title: quant-profiles-vs-dynamic-batching-shape-sweep-march01-2026
content:
Summary:
This note captures a small-sweep benchmark comparing three quantization profiles (fp16, int8-static, int8-dynamic) against our dynamic-batching runtime across different model shapes. The intent: produce concise, shareable guidance for product and SRE on tradeoffs for interactive SLOs vs throughput/cost targets.

Test matrix and hardware:
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (driver 525.xx / CUDA 12) per worker.
- Models: rw-7b-fp16, rw-7b-int8-static, rw-13b-fp16, rw-13b-int8-dynamic. (Note: these are internal build tags.)
- Seq length: prompt 64 + gen 128 = 192 tokens nominal.
- Workloads: 3 shapes: short-chat (prompt 32 / gen 32), interactive (prompt 64 / gen 64), long-turn (prompt 128 / gen 256).
- Batch sizes swept: 1,2,4,8,16. Dynamic batching enabled for all runs (but we record effective batch sizes observed).
- Client load: closed-loop concurrency sweep (1..64) using our load harness (locust-like). Warm runs: 5 minutes warmup, 15 minutes measurement.
- Metrics: p50/p95 latency (ms), throughput (req/s), GPU utilization (%), token-cost estimate ($ per 1M tokens) using internal cost model v2.

Key raw tables (representative slice: interactive shape)
Batch | model                 | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | throughput(req/s) | GPU% | est $/1M tokens
------|-----------------------|---------|---------|-------------------|------|---------------
1     | rw-7b-fp16            | 110     | 200     | 18                | 38   | 62
1     | rw-7b-int8-static     | 95      | 170     | 22                | 35   | 49
4     | rw-7b-fp16            | 150     | 330     | 60                | 72   | 22
4     | rw-7b-int8-static     | 130     | 280     | 75                | 76   | 18
8     | rw-13b-fp16           | 240     | 520     | 38                | 65   | 85
8     | rw-13b-int8-dynamic   | 200     | 420     | 50                | 78   | 62
16    | rw-13b-int8-dynamic   | 370     | 880     | 90                | 92   | 37

Short ASCII chart (p95 vs batch size, interactive shape, rw-7b variants):
Batch -> 1    2    4    8    16
rw-7b-fp16 p95: 200  240  330  460  720
rw-7b-int8 p95: 170  200  280  410  630
Interpretation: quantization consistently reduces p95 by ~15-25% at small-to-medium batch sizes; at very large batches tail multiplies due to queueing and kernel contention.

Throughput efficiency (req/s per GPU%):
- rw-7b-int8-static at batch=4: 75 req/s at 76% -> 0.99 req/s per %-gpu.
- rw-13b-int8-dynamic at batch=8: 50 req/s at 78% -> 0.64 req/s per %-gpu.
Takeaway: smaller models + int8 yield densest token throughput per GPU utilization.

Cost delta estimates (1M tokens):
- Interactive profile (short gen): rw-7b-fp16 -> $62; rw-7b-int8 -> $49 (≈21% cost saving).
- Long-turn heavy gen: savings widen because int8 reduces per-token compute; observed ~28-33% saving on same latency-bounded config.

Observed failure modes and caveats:
- int8-static had lower variance but required per-model calibration; some token-level hallucination/degeneration observed in a small subset of eval prompts (qual notes attached in INF-3412).
- int8-dynamic (runtime quant switching) gives better throughput at mid-large batch sizes but has a higher cold-start overhead due to kernel re-setup (~120-180ms one-time). Impacts SLOs for spiky traffic.
- Dynamic batching across heterogeneous shapes produces bimodal tails: very small requests can sit behind a growing batch and see p95 inflation when traffic spikes. Our batching window + latency cap needs tuning per SLA.

Short recommendation ladder (for product/SRE):
1) Interactive SLOs (p95 target <=200ms): prefer rw-7b-int8-static, batch=1-2, aggressive prefix/KV caching, disable large-batch coalescing.
2) Mixed workloads where cost matters and p95 can be relaxed (<=500ms): enable dynamic quant switching + batch cap 8-16, use int8-dynamic for rw-13b variants.
3) Throughput-first (background embedding or bulk generation): increase batch size to 16–32, prefer int8-static where calibration works — monitor quality regressions.

Operational knobs to add (next steps):
- Add latency-aware batching policy: dynamic window with p95 target as input (policy that bounds batch wait to meet SLA).
- Per-tenant quant profile preferences surfaced in Console (allow opt-in/opt-out).
- Automated micro-eval hook to flag quality drift when switching quant profiles.
- Track cold-start kernel setup times in traces and expose median + p95 in Console.

Open questions:
- What quality delta is acceptable for target customers? Need product to define explicit quality budgets (INF-xxx).
- Is it feasible to auto-fallback to fp16 for a small fraction of tokens that fail a cheap approx-check? (tradeoff: complexity vs quality).

Appendix: short reproducibility notes
- Harness: ./tools/loadtest/sweep --model <tag> --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8,16 --seq 192 --concurrency 1..64 --warm 300 --run 900 --collect gpu_metrics,latency_hist
- Config snapshot: kernel-version: v2.8.3-opt, cudnn 9.x tuned kernels, allocator=jemalloc, batching.window_ms=10 (unless noted).

If this looks useful I can convert the most relevant slices into a one-pager for Product with two charts (p95 vs batch and cost per 1M tokens) and a short ops checklist for production rollout.

Notes-to-self: follow up with Marco on kernel patch for reducing int8 kernel setup from ~120ms -> target <40ms (PR #912).
